findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Auditor cannot yet complete the Whole of Government Accounts work, pending group instructions from the National Audit Office
findings.detail: The paper says the auditor has not received group instructions from the NAO for the Council's WGA submission and cannot start that work. The Council's WGA assurance statement is therefore not yet issued.
findings.matters: The WGA assurance statement is a deadline other councils also depend on, and its delay is a point of reference for finance teams tracking their own submission timetable.
findings.quote: We have not yet received group instructions from the National Audit Office in respect of our work on the Council’s WGA submission.

findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Schools bank balances not reconciled monthly, with the Council to move towards monthly reconciliations during 2026/27
findings.detail: The auditor reports that a school grant payment was posted twice in the ledger, which was not picked up until the year-end reconciliation was provided in February 2026. The Council says it will move towards monthly bank reconciliations for schools during 2026/27.
findings.matters: A duplicate posting caught only at year end is a control gap other councils with school bank accounts may want to test.
findings.quote: The Council do not perform monthly bank reconciliations for Schools accounts and therefore this error was not identified until the year end reconciliation

findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Bad debt provision for Council Tax and Business Rates based on historical data not updated in year, with the Council to implement the recommendation from 2026/27
findings.detail: The auditor reports that the bad debt provision for Council Tax and Business Rates debtors has not been updated in year. The recommendation is that the methodology is reviewed annually, and the Council says it will implement this from 2026/27.
findings.matters: A bad debt provision that is not refreshed in year is a control point other finance directors may want to check against their own provisioning methodology.
findings.quote: The Council’s provision for bad debts on Council Tax and Business Rate debtors is based on historical data which has not been updated in year.

findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Internal audit completed 77% of its 2025/26 plan, with the other 23% relating to ongoing assurance
findings.detail: The paper reports the Chief Internal Auditor's delivery against the 2025/26 plan and a total of 39 completed report-stage audits. The internal audit opinion is that satisfactory assurance can be given on the Council's governance, risk and control framework.
findings.matters: The completion rate and the opinion are the standard measures other audit committees use to judge internal audit delivery.
findings.figures: 77% (plan completed); 23% (ongoing assurance); 39 (completed report-stage audits)
findings.quote: The internal audit function achieved completion of 77% of its plan in 2025/26

findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Pension liability valuation revised after the draft statement of accounts was published, and the accounts were amended
findings.detail: The paper says the actuary issued a revised IAS 19 valuation report after the draft accounts had been published, and that the Council amended its Statement of Accounts to reflect it.
findings.matters: A late change to the IAS 19 pension valuation is a timing risk other finance officers will want to plan for in their own close process.
findings.quote: The Council received a revised IAS 19 valuation report from the actuary after publishing its draft statement of accounts

findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Extrapolated PPE valuation misstatement of £1.72m identified and not adjusted, as management assessed it as not material
findings.detail: The auditor extrapolated a misstatement from sampling of land and building valuations, with the actual error in the sample being £973k. Management has assessed the misstatement as not material and does not plan to adjust it.
findings.matters: The unadjusted misstatement on property valuations is one that other councils' finance directors may need to check against their own asset register controls.
findings.figures: £1.72m (extrapolated misstatement); £973k (actual error in sample)
findings.quote: We identified an extrapolated misstatement of £1.72m from our testing of property, plant and equipment valuations.

findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Auditor has substantially completed work to rebuild assurance over the total reserves balance in the opening balance sheet, using a proof in total approach
findings.detail: The paper says the auditor has adopted a proof in total (PIT) approach to rebuilding assurance and has completed the PPE valuation testing that was outstanding from the 2024/25 audit. It says this work gives assurance over the opening asset balance, and that a return to an unmodified opinion will take several audit cycles.
findings.matters: A council returning to an unmodified opinion after a disclaimer or modified position is a case other finance officers following the same audit backlog will want to track.
findings.quote: we have substantially completed a schedule of work to obtain assurance over the total reserves balance in the Council’s opening balance sheet

findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Auditor on track to issue the audit opinion on the 2025/26 accounts in November 2026
findings.detail: The paper says the audit of the financial statements is still in progress and the audit opinion is expected in November 2026.
findings.matters: The timing of the opinion is a milestone for the Council's accounts, and the paper gives the date explicitly.
findings.figures: November 2026
findings.quote: We are on track to complete our work and issue our audit opinion in November 2026.

findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account outturn was a surplus of £2.7m in 2025/26, transferred to the HRA reserve
findings.detail: The paper reports the HRA surplus for 2025/26 and says it was transferred to the HRA reserve.
findings.matters: The HRA surplus being added to reserves is a movement finance directors at other councils with HRAs can compare with their own outturn.
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account (HRA) outturn was a surplus of £2.7m in 2025/26, with this being transferred to the HRA reserve.

findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Usable reserves of £267.3m at 31/03/2026, with £100.9m under General Fund or General Fund Support reserves
findings.detail: The paper says the Council's reserves could offset both the projected DSG deficit for 2026/27 and the projected deficit at the end of the statutory override period. It also says the Council is recasting its reserves to correct categorisation.
findings.matters: The reserves figure is the buffer the paper relies on to absorb the DSG deficit, which is a comparison point for finance directors in councils with similar exposures.
findings.figures: £267.3m (Usable Reserves); £100.9m (General Fund and General Fund Support reserves)
findings.quote: there were £267.3m of Usable Reserves at 31/03/2026, with £100.9m of these reserves falling under the General Fund or General Fund Support reserves earmarked by the Council

findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Council Tax rise of 4.99% agreed for 2026/27, raising an additional £8.2m
findings.detail: The paper says the Council Tax increase for 2026/27 was agreed and raises an additional £8.2m, which is in addition to the gaps the MTFP shows for later years.
findings.matters: The income raised from the Council Tax rise is a specific number other finance directors can use when benchmarking their own 2026/27 income assumptions.
findings.quote: which was agreed by the Council for 26/27 raising an additional £8.2m for the Council.

findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Budget gaps of £10.9m for 2027/28 and £8.7m for 2028/29 remain in the MTFP, before any Council Tax rise
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget and MTFP to 2028/29 are balanced for 2026/27 but show gaps in the following two years. The paper says these gaps do not assume a Council Tax rise, and that further efficiencies are still needed to balance future budgets.
findings.matters: A council with multi-year gaps that depend on further efficiencies is one whose savings delivery over the next two years is worth comparing with peers.
findings.quote: In this plan, there is a budget gap of £10.9m for 2027/28, and a gap of £8.7m has been identified for 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Interest payable underspent by £5m in 2025/26 because capital expenditure was reprofiled
findings.detail: The paper attributes part of the Corporate Budgets underspend to lower interest payable, linked to the reprofiling of capital expenditure.
findings.matters: Interest underspends that come from slower capital spend are timing effects rather than savings, which is relevant to anyone reading the Council's borrowing position.
findings.quote: and an underspend in the level of interest payable of £5m due to the reprofiling of capital expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Children's Services overspent by £12.1m in 2025/26, offset by a £13.2m underspend within Corporate Budgets
findings.detail: The paper says the Corporate Budgets underspend came from achieved efficiency targets, an unbudgeted dividend from Manchester Airport Car Park Loan, a government grant on redistribution of business rates surpluses, and lower interest payable. The Children's Services overspend was in line with the Month 9 projection.
findings.matters: The overspend was offset by one-off or non-service income, which is a dependency other councils will want to test against their own corporate budget headroom.
findings.figures: £12.1m (Children's Services overspend); £13.2m (Corporate Budgets underspend)
findings.quote: The underspend in Corporate Budgets was offset by a £12.1m overspend within Children’s Services, which was in line with the Council’s projection at Month 9

findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Revenue outturn for 2025/26 was an overall underspend of £0.065m
findings.detail: The paper reports the 2025/26 revenue outturn as a small overall underspend, which was transferred to earmarked reserves that fall within General Fund support. This net figure sits on top of a large gross movement between Corporate Budgets and Children's Services.
findings.matters: A net underspend that hides large gross offsetting variances is a pattern finance directors elsewhere will want to compare with their own outturns.
findings.figures: £0.065m overall underspend
findings.quote: which reported its revenue outturn position for 2025/26 as an overall underspend of £0.065m

findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: High Needs Block cumulative overspend rose from £16m to £34m in 2025/26, with the DSG reserve deficit moving from £9.7m to £25.9m by the end of 2024/25
findings.detail: The paper says the DSG reserve opened 2024/25 with a £9.7m deficit and reached £25.9m by the end of that year. It attributes the rise mainly to the High Needs Block overspend, partly offset by underspends on other DSG blocks.
findings.matters: The paper ties the rise in the deficit to rising demand for costly, complex support for children with special educational needs, which is a pressure other councils' finance officers will recognise.
findings.figures: £9.7m (opening DSG reserve deficit); £25.9m (end of 2024/25); £16m to £34m (High Needs Block cumulative overspend)
findings.quote: This was largely driven by the cumulative overspend on the High Needs Block increasing from £16m to £34m in 2025/26

findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Projected DSG deficits of £15.6m for 2026/27 and £17.9m for 2027/28, leaving a £36.1m deficit at the end of the statutory override period
findings.detail: The SEND Reform Plan projects in-year DSG deficits up to 2027/28, the end of the statutory override period. The paper states the resulting overall deficit position at the end of that period.
findings.matters: The statutory override ending is a hard point at which the DSG deficit has to be funded from the Council's own resources, which is a liability other councils with DSG deficits will also face.
findings.figures: £15.6m (2026/27); £17.9m (2027/28); £36.1m (overall at end of statutory override)
findings.quote: The Council has projected DSG deficits of £15.6m and £17.9m for 2026/27 and 2027/28 respectively, which would leave an overall deficit position of £36.1m at the end of the statutory override period.

findings.paper_title: Wigan MBC - Draft Auditors Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: SEND Reform Plan approved on 2 October 2026, making the Council eligible for a High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of its DSG deficit
findings.detail: The paper says the Department for Education approved the Council's Local SEND Reform Plan, which makes the Council eligible for the grant. The paper says payment is expected on 30/11/2026 and would reduce the overall DSG deficit at 31/03/2026 to £2.6m.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council with a DSG deficit can see the grant route the Council used to cut its deficit, and the conditions attached to it.
findings.figures: 90%; £2.6m; payment expected 30/11/2026
findings.quote: The Council received notification on 2ndOctober 2026 that the SEND Reform Plan had been approved

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring – Half Yearly Review
findings.headline: Proposed investment limits would raise the local authority counterparty limit to £20m, and the Money Market Fund limit from £45m to £80m overall and £15m to £20m per fund.
findings.detail: The paper says the current Money Market Fund limit is periodically reached, which forces surplus cash into instant-access bank accounts. It estimates that the rate differential can be up to 0.5%, resulting in a potential loss of investment income. The local authority counterparty limit currently stands at £10m per authority, with £5m per transaction.
findings.matters: These changes raise the Council's allowed exposure to other local authorities and money market funds, and a finance director at another council can compare their own limits and the income they forgo when those limits bind.
findings.figures: £45 million current overall MMF limit; £80 million proposed overall MMF limit; £15 million current per-fund limit; £20 million proposed per-fund limit; £10m current local authority limit; £20 million proposed local authority limit; up to 0.5% rate differential
findings.quote: It is therefore proposed that the overall Money Market Fund limit is increased from £45 million to £80 million and that the limit per fund is increased from £15 million to £20 million.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring – Half Yearly Review
findings.headline: Proposed policy change would set the maximum limit for each debt maturity band at 30%, where the under-12-months band is currently 15%.
findings.detail: The paper says the under-12-months limit sitting below the 20% limit for the one-to-two-year band could cause a technical breach through the passage of time alone. It also says the low limits in shorter bands may restrict access to shorter-term borrowing, which can be cheaper in some market conditions. The change is for approval by Council.
findings.matters: A council raising its short-term borrowing ceiling is signalling a change in its refinancing approach, which lenders and peers with similar maturity limits will want to see.
findings.figures: 15% current under-12-months limit; 30% proposed limit for each band; 40% current 40-to-50-year limit reduced to 30%
findings.quote: It is therefore proposed that the maximum limit for each maturity band is changed to 30%.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring – Half Yearly Review
findings.headline: MUFG Corporate Markets forecasts Bank Rate peaking at 4.0% and falling to 3.25% by March 2028, after Bank Rate was held at 3.75% through the period.
findings.detail: The paper notes market expectations of a peak between 4.5% and 4.75%, but MUFG forecasts a lower peak. MUFG's reasoning is that a potential increase of more than 20% in the energy price cap from January, combined with rising mortgage rates, may weaken household spending.
findings.matters: The rate outlook sets the cost assumptions a council uses when planning the £100.000m of new borrowing, and peers and lenders will compare it with their own forecasts.
findings.figures: 4.0% forecast peak Bank Rate; 3.25% by March 2028; 3.75% Bank Rate maintained; 4.5% to 4.75% market-expected peak range
findings.quote: On this basis, MUFG Corporate Markets forecast that Bank Rate will peak at 4.0% before gradually falling to 3.25% by March 2028.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring – Half Yearly Review
findings.headline: No debt rescheduling has been undertaken in the current financial year to date.
findings.detail: The paper defines debt rescheduling as repaying loans early and replacing them with new borrowing on different terms. It reports none in 2026/27 so far.
findings.matters: A council that has not restructured its debt is holding its existing maturity and rate profile, which is the baseline a lender or peer would compare any future rescheduling against.
findings.quote: No debt rescheduling has been undertaken during the current financial year.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring – Half Yearly Review
findings.headline: Capital expenditure is forecast at £176.715m against a £240.077m original estimate, and external debt at 31 March 2027 is now forecast £29.869m lower than originally estimated, primarily from slippage within the capital programme.
findings.detail: The paper says the reduction in forecast debt is primarily due to slippage within the capital programme. It also says the level of under-borrowing remains broadly unchanged, meaning the Council has continued to use internal cash balances to fund part of its borrowing requirement.
findings.matters: Capital slippage lowers the external borrowing a council needs to raise, and it shows how the timing of capital spending is feeding through to the amount of debt a lender will be asked to provide.
findings.figures: £240.077m original capital expenditure estimate; £176.715m Q2 revised forecast; £29.869m lower external debt than originally estimated
findings.quote: Although external debt as at 31 March 2027 is now forecast to be £29.869m lower than originally estimated, primarily due to slippage within the capital programme

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring – Half Yearly Review
findings.headline: External debt is forecast to rise by £90.610m to £574.795m by 31 March 2027, including £100.000m of new borrowing planned for the second half of the year.
findings.detail: The net increase in borrowing is £93.182m. This combines £100.000m of new borrowing with £20.000m of refinancing for maturing PWLB loans, offset by £26.818m of scheduled loan repayments.
findings.matters: A council planning £100.000m of new borrowing in six months is a source of demand for lenders, and its refinancing timing is relevant to peers managing similar maturity profiles.
findings.figures: £90.610m expected increase in external debt; £574.795m expected debt at 31 March 2027; £93.182m net increase in borrowing; £100.000m new borrowing; £20.000m refinancing; £26.818m scheduled repayments
findings.quote: The revised forecast indicates that the Council’s external debt is expected to increase by £90.610m to £574.795m by 31 March 2027.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring – Half Yearly Review
findings.headline: Average return on investments was 3.92% in the first six months of 2026/27, against a 7-Day Compounded SONIA rate of 3.73%, a difference of 0.19%.
findings.detail: The paper says the Council overperformed the benchmark by 0.19%. Average funds available for investment over the first six months were £91.455m, and investments held at 30 September 2026 were £86.900m.
findings.matters: A council reporting its return against SONIA gives peers and lenders a like-for-like measure of cash management performance.
findings.figures: 3.92% average interest rate; 3.73% 7-Day Compounded SONIA; 0.19% outperformance; £91.455m average funds available; £86.900m investments at 30/09/2026
findings.quote: The average interest rate obtained by the Council during this period was 3.92%, the published 7-Day Compounded SONIA rate was 3.73%, therefore the Council overperformed by 0.19%.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring – Half Yearly Review
findings.headline: Financing and investment income is forecast at £1.554m favourable to budget at year end, as at Quarter 2 2026/27.
findings.detail: The favourable position is mainly from lower than budgeted PWLB interest costs and higher than anticipated treasury investment income. Additional variances come from a higher than budgeted C-Share dividend from Manchester Airport Holding Ltd relating to the Drop & Go Car Park, and an unbudgeted YPO dividend.
findings.matters: Treasury activity is adding to the revenue budget, and a finance director at another council can compare the sources of that headroom against their own treasury and dividend income.
findings.figures: £1.554m favourable to budget at year end
findings.quote: At Quarter 2, financing and investment income is forecast to be approximately £1.554m favourable to budget at year end.

findings.headline: The auditor records draft accounts received on 30 June 2026 as being of good quality.
findings.detail: The auditor says the finance team gave timely responses to queries and that the working papers were of good quality. Audit work is substantially complete, with payroll, cash and the Whole of Government Accounts remaining outstanding.
findings.matters: Finance team capacity and the quality of draft accounts are a benchmark for other finance directors assessing how their own closedown is going.
findings.figures: Draft accounts received 30 June 2026
findings.quote: Draft accounts were received from the Council on 30 June 2026 and were of a good quality.

findings.headline: Forvis Mazars has not identified any significant weaknesses in Wigan's arrangements for value for money in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The auditor has made no recommendations on value for money. Its commentary will appear in the Auditor's Annual Report, which it intends to issue in November 2026. The draft audit report confirms no matters to report on significant weaknesses.
findings.matters: Value-for-money findings show whether the auditor sees weak arrangements in financial sustainability, governance or performance, which other councils and lenders also assess.
findings.figures: None stated in the paper
findings.quote: we have not identified any significant weaknesses in arrangements

findings.headline: Forvis Mazars has identified no significant deficiencies in internal control and reports one further control observation on bad debt provisions.
findings.detail: The bad debt provision for Council Tax and Business Rates is based on historical data that has not been updated in the year. The auditor recommends an annual update to the methodology, and management will implement this from 2026/27. A separate observation covers monthly bank reconciliations for school accounts, which management will move towards during 2026/27.
findings.matters: How council tax and business rates bad debts are provided for affects the income figures that lenders rely on.
findings.figures: None stated in the paper
findings.quote: The Council’s provision for bad debts on Council Tax and Business Rate debtors is based on historical data which has not been updated in year.

findings.headline: The Council received a revised IAS 19 pension valuation from its actuary after publishing its draft accounts and amended the Statement of Accounts to reflect it.
findings.detail: The revised valuation arrived in July 2026. The Council updated Note 40 to match it. The paper states that this had no net impact on the pension liability in the draft accounts.
findings.matters: Late changes to the net pension liability are relevant to anyone reading the balance sheet, and to councils with similar pension funds.
findings.figures: None stated in the paper
findings.quote: The Council received a revised IAS 19 valuation report from the actuary after publishing its draft statement of accounts

findings.headline: The auditor flags a disclosure issue with DSG deficits, which were transferred to the DSG Adjustment Account via Earmarked Reserves.
findings.detail: The auditor identified that the DSG deficit was moved through Earmarked Reserves rather than directly from the General Fund. The auditor is waiting for an updated 2025/26 statement of accounts to confirm the correction, and will report on it in a follow-up letter.
findings.matters: The presentation of DSG deficits in reserves is a live question for councils nationally, and a finance officer at another council would want to see how this one is being corrected.
findings.figures: None stated in the paper
findings.quote: with the deficits being incorrectly transferred to the DSG Adjustment Account via Earmarked Reserves rather than directly from the General Fund account

findings.headline: Forvis Mazars identified an extrapolated £1.72m misstatement in property, plant and equipment valuations, which management has left unadjusted.
findings.detail: Three of the sixty revalued land and buildings samples had different values in the asset register from those calculated by the external valuer. The actual error in those samples was £973k, which the auditor extrapolated across the untested population. Management has assessed the misstatement as not material and does not plan to adjust it.
findings.matters: A finance director will want to see how valuation errors in the asset register are being handled, and the balance sheet effect of the unadjusted amount.
findings.figures: Extrapolated misstatement £1.72m (£1,720k); actual error in samples £973k; overall materiality £24,800k; performance materiality £17,300k
findings.quote: We identified an extrapolated misstatement of £1.72m from our testing of property, plant and equipment valuations.

findings.headline: The auditor describes 2025/26 as the first of a three-year rebuilding period, with an unmodified opinion targeted for 2027/28.
findings.detail: Rebuilding assurance covers the opening balance sheet and reserves, and the auditor says it has substantially completed this work. It has gained assurance over the opening balance of assets after finishing its property, plant and equipment valuation testing, which it had not completed in the 2024/25 audit.
findings.matters: Other councils recovering from disclaimers will be tracking the same timetable, and lenders will want the expected date for a clean audit opinion.
findings.figures: Unmodified opinion expected in 2027/28
findings.quote: 2025/26 is the first of a three-year rebuilding period

findings.headline: Forvis Mazars anticipates issuing a qualified opinion on Wigan's 2025/26 statement of accounts, in line with its June 2026 audit plan.
findings.detail: The auditor says its procedures are substantially complete and that it expects a qualified opinion, as planned. The qualification relates to the disclaimers of opinion issued for 2023/24 and 2024/25 because there was insufficient time to obtain evidence before the backstop dates. The specified backstop date for 2025/26 is 31 January 2027.
findings.matters: A finance director at Wigan or elsewhere will want to know how far the qualification follows from the backstop regime rather than from new problems in the 2025/26 accounts.
findings.figures: Backstop date for 2025/26: 31 January 2027
findings.quote: we anticipate issuing a qualified opinion in line with our plan

findings.headline: General Fund balances being rebuilt with £2.5m added in 2026/27 and £1m annual contributions planned 2027/28 onwards, but still modest relative to budget gaps.
findings.detail: Council transferred £2.5m into General Fund balances in 2026/27 and plans further £1m annual contributions. This is intended to strengthen resilience and capacity to manage emerging risks. Earmarked reserves estimated at £58.9m at 31 March 2027. Use of reserves for one-off expenditure reduced significantly in 2025/26, reflecting commitment to sustainable reserve levels. However, reserve building remains modest relative to £8.5m–£18.9m annual savings requirements.
findings.matters: Deliberate attempt to strengthen financial resilience, but constrained by budget gaps; shows management discipline but relative insufficiency.
findings.figures: £2.5m transferred 2026/27; £1m planned annual contributions 2027/28 onwards; £58.9m earmarked reserves at 31 March 2027
findings.quote: the Council transferred £2.5m into General Fund balances during 2026/27 and plans to make further contributions of £1m in 2027/28 and subsequent years.

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility income of £6m per annum expected to reduce as packaging sector adapts; Deposit Return Scheme (October 2027) will further reduce recycling income.
findings.detail: EPR scheme currently yields council £6m annually. As producers respond to EPR requirements through packaging reduction and substitution, this income stream is forecast to decline (amount unquantified). Separately, Deposit Return Scheme commencing October 2027 will remove valuable drinks containers from local authority recycling streams, reducing income further and increasing processing costs. Council has also accelerated collection of flexible plastics (April 2026), though national mandate was postponed to 2030.
findings.matters: Material income source at risk; compound effect of two policy changes reducing recycling income and increasing costs; forecast impact on budget not yet quantified.
findings.figures: £6m per annum from EPR (at risk); DRS commencing October 2027
findings.quote: Presently under this scheme we receive around £6m per annum for dealing with this waste. This may reduce as the sector responds to the changes.

findings.headline: Maintained mainstream schools' financial position deteriorated, with 50 of 86 schools in in-year deficit and 11 in cumulative deficit in 2025/26.
findings.detail: Schools' aggregate balances fell £0.669m in 2025/26 despite being the largest sector. Falling pupil numbers (149 fewer primary, 76 fewer secondary in October 2025 census) will reduce funding allocations further. Council is providing support to schools in cumulative deficit, but sector-wide pressure is evident and structural (not cyclical), given demographic decline.
findings.matters: Delegated budget sector in stress; indicates schools cannot absorb cost pressures; falling pupil numbers are structural not temporary; potential for growing council support requirement.
findings.figures: 50 of 86 schools in in-year deficit; 11 in cumulative deficit; balances down £0.669m in 2025/26; 149 fewer primary pupils, 76 fewer secondary pupils in October 2025 census
findings.quote: In 2025/26 Maintained mainstream schools' balances reduced by £0.669m, with 50 of the 86 schools reporting in-year deficits.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review delivered lower funding growth to Wigan than comparable authorities; Business Rates Retention reset redistributed 13 years of accumulated growth.
findings.detail: The December 2025 Fair Funding Review reassessed resource allocation across councils using updated needs assessment. Wigan's outcome was lower funding growth than many peers, reflecting lower relative needs assessment. Business Rates Retention Scheme was reset for the first time since April 2013; accumulated business rates growth since 2013 was redistributed to other councils in line with new assessment. This is a structural change in Wigan's funding trajectory relative to peers.
findings.matters: Structural weakening of Wigan's funding position relative to comparators; limits council's flexibility versus peer councils; no recovery mechanism.
findings.figures: Lower funding growth than comparable authorities (specific differential not disclosed); business rates reset after 13 years of retention.
findings.quote: the revised funding arrangements have resulted in Wigan receiving a lower level of funding growth than many comparable authorities.

findings.headline: High Needs Block projected to overspend £17.5m (2026/27) and £17.9m (2027/28), driven by EHCP growth and out-of-borough independent school placements.
findings.detail: High Needs overspend is driven by rising numbers and complexity of pupils at maintained special schools, EHCP growth, high-cost out-of-borough independent school placements, and post-16 SEND. The council is implementing an Inclusion and SEND Strategic Plan, but full impact will take time. These are recurring annual overspends, not one-off pressures.
findings.matters: Ongoing structural overspend; indicates capacity and pricing challenge in SEND provision; feeds DSG deficit tracked separately but will merge into General Fund post-2028.
findings.figures: £17.547m projected overspend 2026/27; £17.979m projected overspend 2027/28
findings.quote: The current projection is for an overspend in 26/27 of £17.547m and an overspend of £17.979m in 27/28.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £25.9m, with High Needs Stability Grant covering only 90%, leaves £2.6m unfunded and future support uncertain post-March 2028.
findings.detail: DSG cumulative deficit at 31 March 2026 was £25.934m, driven by £34.028m High Needs Block overspend. Government High Needs Stability Grant will cover 90% (approx. £23.3m), leaving council responsible for £2.593m. Government has not confirmed further support for deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28; council estimates approx. £3.5m additional liability across those years. Statutory override separating DSG from general fund budget ends 31 March 2028, at which point unfunded DSG becomes a core budget issue.
findings.matters: Material unfunded liability outside main revenue budget; government support commitment ends 2028; deficit may then flow directly into General Fund budget gap.
findings.figures: £25.934m cumulative deficit; £34.028m High Needs Block overspend; £2.593m council shortfall post-grant; projected £3.5m additional liability 2026/27–2027/28
findings.quote: As at the 31 March 26 the Council's DSG position has an overall deficit of £25.934m as a result of the cumulative overspend on the High Needs Block of £34.028m... the Government will award the Authority a High Needs Stability Grant to cover 90% of the local authorities' overall DSG deficit... This will still leave a deficit amount of £2.593m to be funded by Wigan Council.

findings.headline: Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP) numbers have more than doubled since 2018/19, with 14% annual growth forecast through 2029, driving Home to School Transport cost escalation.
findings.detail: EHCP numbers grew over 100% since 2018/19 and have accelerated, with 18% growth in the year to June 2026 alone. Projections show 14% annual growth continuing through 2029. This is the key driver of Home to School Transport cost growth. The council has an action plan (post-16 policy, independent travel training, route optimization) but effectiveness is unproven. The growth is linked to national SEND reform impacts.
findings.matters: Fastest-growing cost pressure with no clear ceiling; driven partly by national policy rather than local factors; mitigation plan's success is undemonstrated.
findings.figures: >100% growth since 2018/19; 18% growth July 2025–June 2026; 14% annual growth projected through 2029
findings.quote: There has been an increase of over 100% in the number of children with an EHCP plans in Wigan since 2018/19. From July 2025 to June 2026 there has been an increase of 18% in EHCP numbers, and whilst the full impact of the Schools White Paper and SEND reforms takes effect, it is still projected that the annual growth will be 14% through to 2029.

findings.headline: Adult social care faces fastest-aging population in Greater Manchester, with 16% growth forecast in over-80s, compounding demand and cost pressures.
findings.detail: Wigan's over-80 population is forecast to grow 16% over the plan period—faster than other Greater Manchester authorities. This is combined with growth in younger adults requiring long-term care, hospital discharge pressures, and rising care sector wages and fees. The council is applying budget growth to social care and focusing on transformation around early intervention and prevention, but aging population is structural.
findings.matters: Structural demographic pressure not easily managed through short-term efficiency; directly affects service cost trajectory and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: 16% increase forecast in number of over-80-year-olds supported over the MTFP period
findings.quote: Wigan has the fastest ageing population in Greater Manchester, with the numbers of older people in the Borough forecast to rise over the next three years with a 16% increase in the number of over 80-year-olds supported.

findings.headline: Children Looked After increased 29% from 533 (March 2020) to 687 (July 2026), with high-cost external placements remaining a significant financial risk.
findings.detail: Numbers have grown from 533 to 687 in just over 6 years, driven by pandemic legacy impacts and socio-economic challenges. The council is implementing a Children First transformation strategy (2023–2028) to reduce placements through early help and family support, but timeframe for cost stabilization unclear. Continued reliance on expensive external residential placements is identified as an ongoing financial risk.
findings.matters: Major cost driver with uncertain resolution timeline; council betting on transformation strategy to deliver cost avoidance.
findings.quote: The number of Children Looked After by Wigan Council has increased by 29%, from 533 in March 2020 to 687 in July 2026, reflecting growing levels of need across the borough.

findings.headline: Budget gaps of £8.5m, £18.9m and £13.9m forecast for 2027/28–2029/30, requiring significant annual savings.
findings.detail: The MTFP forecasts growing annual shortfalls between available funding and budget requirement. The council has not yet identified the specific savings to close these gaps; these are baseline requirements ahead of detailed efficiency planning. The gaps reflect both increased budget pressures (particularly in social care and SEND) and lower funding growth than comparable authorities following the Fair Funding Review.
findings.matters: Escalating annual efficiency targets indicate structural funding-demand mismatch; council enters budget cycle without settled solution.
findings.figures: £8,458k (2027/28), £18,972k (2028/29), £13,924k (2029/30) base savings requirement. Actual budget gaps are larger: £8,458k, £27,430k, £41,353k.
findings.quote: Based upon the current assumptions the following gap in finances has been identified. These figures will be updated during the year as estimates become more certain. Budget Gap 2027/28 £8,458k, 2028/29 £18,972k, 2029/30 £13,924k.

findings.headline: Adult and children's social care demand is rising while inflationary and pay pressures compound costs.
findings.detail: The council describes significant financial challenges from increasing service demand in adult and children's social care combined with ongoing inflationary and pay pressures. The document does not quantify the demand growth, cost increases, funding gap in these services, or the plan to address them.
findings.matters: Adult and children's social care are the largest costs for most councils. Rising demand colliding with pay inflation creates structural budget pressure that resists one-off efficiency solutions. Lenders need to know whether a council has a credible long-term answer to rising social care costs or is managing them through year-on-year deficit and drawdown of reserves.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The Council continues to face significant financial challenges arising from increasing service demand, particularly in Adult and Children's Social Care, alongside ongoing inflationary and pay pressures.

findings.headline: Construction cost inflation and increased borrowing costs are compressing the affordability of capital investment.
findings.detail: The council identifies construction cost inflation, limited capital resources and increased borrowing costs as pressures requiring prioritised deployment of capital. The document does not specify which schemes are at risk, what capital spend the council expects to need, or what the cost of replacement borrowing is compared to existing debt.
findings.matters: Rising borrowing costs directly increase debt servicing charges and shrink resources available for service delivery. Councils that cannot afford planned capital investment face delivery delays. Higher borrowing costs also increase refinancing risk on maturing debt.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Ongoing pressures arising from construction cost inflation, limited capital resources and increased borrowing costs require continued prioritisation to ensure that investment remains affordable and sustainable.

findings.headline: Service expenditure reductions will be necessary over the next three years.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that reductions to service spending will be required over the medium term. The document does not specify the size of the budget gap, which services are affected, or the savings programme to close it. This is the opening statement of a budget under stress, but without quantification or solution detail.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know whether a council has acknowledged and can address emerging budget deficits. An explicit statement of required reductions signals financial difficulty; omitting it would be worse, but specific numbers and closure plans would be more credible.
findings.figures: three years
findings.quote: Service expenditure reductions will be necessary over the next three years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Detailed Capital Programme and Resourcing 2026-27 - 2028-29
findings.headline: Capital programme is heavily front-loaded to 2026/27 at £190.7m (41% of three-year total), creating concentrated cash-flow requirements.
findings.detail: Spending is concentrated in 2026/27 at £190.7m, declining to £181.9m in 2027/28 and £91.9m in 2028/29. This front-loaded profile means the council faces substantial immediate cash-flow requirements in the coming 12 months to fund capital projects and associated borrowing drawdowns. Major 2026/27 spending lines include Economy & Regeneration (£85.9m, mostly town centre), HRA housing (£46.5m), Children & Young People (£20.8m), and Culture (£13.2m). Any project slippage would push spending into later years, affecting the forecasted profile.
findings.matters: Concentrated capital spending creates specific borrowing and cash-flow requirements in 2026/27; finance director needs to ensure cash management capacity; lender needs to understand timing of debt drawdowns

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Detailed Capital Programme and Resourcing 2026-27 - 2028-29
findings.headline: Haigh Hall cultural investment of £42.5m combines grants with £22.3m prudential borrowing for heritage site redevelopment.
findings.detail: Haigh Hall is a £42.5m cultural and heritage project in the capital programme spanning 2026-29, with expenditure accelerating in 2027/28 (£11.2m) and 2028/29 (£13.5m). Funding combines government grant (DLUHC LUF: £8.9m), Heritage Lottery Fund grant (£2.5m), and prudential borrowing (£22.3m). This represents significant investment in a non-revenue-generating cultural asset, requiring ongoing debt service from the general fund rather than from project income.
findings.matters: Large borrowing for heritage assets creates ongoing revenue pressure; lender needs to understand these differ from income-generating investments and affect general fund affordability
findings.figures: Haigh Hall £42.5m total; DLUHC grant £8.9m; Heritage Lottery £2.5m; prudential borrowing £22.3m

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Detailed Capital Programme and Resourcing 2026-27 - 2028-29
findings.headline: GAL Town Centre Investment Framework represents £156m investment with £96.4m prudential borrowing, concentrating £57.6m (38% of project) in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The Economy & Regeneration directorate is undertaking the GAL Town Centre Investment Framework as its largest capital commitment. The project totals £156m with highly concentrated near-term spending: £57.6m in 2026/27 alone. Funding is provided by £96.4m prudential borrowing (61% of total) and £48.2m government grants (DLUHC Levelling Up Fund and Long-Term Plan for Towns). This major strategic investment creates a substantial debt service obligation on future revenue.
findings.matters: Capital investments of this scale and borrowing intensity require lender confidence in delivery, market conditions, and financial sustainability; concentration in single year creates immediate cash-flow pressure
